title: Building Blocks
subtitle: How a result I never set as a goal came out of stacked foundations
thesis: I build platforms and models, not products or specific numbers. Weak foundations in life, tech, marketing, or finance mean nothing lasting gets built.
thesis_note: the belief this chapter is built on; not a measured result
summary: A nonfiction interlude in Clark Huang's own voice: his fitness journey from a 2018 wake-up through Orangetheory, CrossFit, gymnastics skills like the ring muscle-up and double unders, half triathlons and a full triathlon, and six official marathons, including a 3:03:55 Boston qualifier at 47 that he never set as a goal when he started. The result came out of stacked foundations. He still calls himself a C player in CrossFit. A light turn toward Chapter 36, on how companies should use AI, closes the chapter.
preview: In 2018 I was building platforms for other people and had built no foundation for myself: I was not feeling good about my body, I had gained weight without realizing it, and I was always tired. A Dale Carnegie vision-board exercise produced a triathlon I had not planned, along with learning guitar, picking piano back up, retiring by 50, and some business-specific things. I learned the next step as I needed it: Orangetheory in 2019, CrossFit 9 within six months, a Level 1 certification in 2022. CrossFit is largely gymnastics-focused; a ring muscle-up took years of practice, and double unders that hold up under fatigue took six years. Running, swimming, and the bike were ladders too. I did half triathlons, then a full triathlon — a 2.4-mile swim, a 112-mile bike, and a 26.2-mile run after that. Official marathon results then tell more of the stack: a first marathon of 5:56:24 in 2021, 3:25:45 in 2022, a 3:03:55 Boston qualifier at 47 in 2023, a Carlsbad half at sub-three-hour marathon pace, and Boston itself in 2024, “not my fastest but definitely the FUNNEST.” I qualified for the 2024 Age-Group Quarterfinals and did the workouts unofficially, scaled, after Boston. The point is the stack, not the number. Chapter 36 takes the same idea to how a company should use AI.
hook: A nonfiction interlude in Clark's own voice: a fitness journey whose best result was never the original goal, and came out of stacked foundations.
rule: Build the foundation, not the number. Learn the next step when you need it. Practice the core movements until they are yours, then put them in combination. Keep going. Let the result emerge from the work you stacked, and measure the work you actually did. The same rule holds in life, in tech, in marketing, and in finance: if the foundation is weak, nothing lasting gets built. When you later apply AI to that work, put it on fundamentals you already understand.
frame: Nonfiction, in the author's own voice, not Charlie Hack's. This is Clark Huang's own fitness journey, with official race results for the running events named in the chapter. Half triathlons and the full triathlon are kept unnamed. The employer is described generically, not by company name. Not affiliated with or endorsed by CrossFit, Orangetheory Fitness, REVEL, or the Boston Athletic Association; those names are used only as facts about training and races he did.
